title: Evaluation and Observability: Evidence for Shipping LLM Systems
summary: Build defensible evaluation datasets, quantify paired improvements, calibrate judges, and connect task quality to production traces and release decisions.
learningObjectives: Design contamination-resistant evaluation splits and representative task slices.
Calculate and interpret uncertainty for paired model comparisons.
Choose exact, semantic, and judge-based metrics with explicit failure modes.
Connect task outcomes, serving SLOs, traces, and token accounting.
Define canary gates and a privacy-aware production feedback loop.

sections.title: Start with a decision and a measurement contract
paragraphs: Evaluation estimates whether a system meets a task requirement; observability explains what happened while it ran. A fluent answer, a successful HTTP response, and a completed user task are different outcomes. For a support assistant, success might require an answer grounded in the authorized policy, a valid citation, and correct escalation when evidence is missing. Define the unit of evaluation as a complete conversation or workflow when earlier actions affect later outcomes.

Before comparing candidates, write down the target population, eligible requests, success rubric, unacceptable failures, and decision threshold. Record the model identifier, prompt version, retrieval index snapshot, tool versions, decoding settings, and evaluator version. These form the experimental treatment. A prompt change and a new document corpus together cannot establish which change caused the improvement. Use component tests to diagnose failures and end-to-end tests to decide whether the complete system is useful.

Keep a metric hierarchy: business outcome, task-quality indicators, and diagnostic measurements. Resolution without recontact is an outcome; grounded answer accuracy is a task indicator; retrieval recall is diagnostic. Improving retrieval recall can still worsen answers through distracting context. Aggregate utility can guide optimization, but a weighted score should never hide a violated authorization or privacy constraint.

sections.title: Construct datasets that survive contact with development
paragraphs: Build the evaluation set from representative, permitted examples plus deliberately difficult cases: unanswerable questions, conflicting documents, long conversations, malformed tool results, and rare costly errors. Store input provenance, expected behavior, labels, slice tags, and annotation instructions. Adjudicate disagreements between annotators rather than assuming one label is ground truth. Keep a representative set for estimating average performance and a separate stress suite for exposing failure modes; their sampling distributions answer different questions.

Split by the source of dependence. Questions paraphrased from one document, messages from one customer, and variants of one template belong together. Random row splitting can leak nearly identical problems across development and test. Use development data for prompt selection, a locked release set for candidate decisions, and a later temporal holdout for changing traffic. A protected set gradually becomes development data if engineers repeatedly inspect its failures and tune against them.

Contamination includes exact benchmark overlap, paraphrases, answer keys, and indirect exposure through tuning or evaluator examples. The GPT-3 paper documents why training-data overlap complicates benchmark interpretation. Normalize and deduplicate known corpora, inspect semantic near-duplicates, and track access to private tests. These controls reduce known leakage; they cannot prove that an opaque pretrained model never encountered a public example. Fresh private tasks improve evidence but also need representative difficulty and stable labeling.

diagram.title: Three dataset roles
diagram.caption: Partition related examples together before assigning roles; do not move failures into training while claiming the same test remains untouched.

nodes.label: Development
nodes.detail: Visible examples support iteration, rubric refinement, and prompt selection.

nodes.label: Locked release
nodes.detail: Restricted examples support a predefined decision after candidate selection.

nodes.label: Temporal audit
nodes.detail: Later traffic detects whether the original evaluation still represents production.

sections.title: Match the evaluator to the claim
paragraphs: Exact checks are strongest when correctness has an executable definition: schema validity, numerical tolerance, required fields, or passing isolated tests. Normalize only irrelevant differences. Removing punctuation from a product identifier could erase a meaningful error. Tests also need coverage: code that passes three examples has not thereby satisfied its complete specification. Validate tool side effects and authorization separately from the text that describes them.

Semantic metrics tolerate valid paraphrases. BERTScore compares contextual token embeddings between generated and reference text, which is useful when surface wording varies. Similarity remains a proxy: changing a dosage, negating a claim, or citing the wrong document can preserve much of the surrounding meaning. Evaluate factual assertions against evidence and inspect numerical entities explicitly. A reference answer can itself be incomplete, so multiple acceptable outcomes or a rubric may be needed.

LLM judges can score open-ended qualities such as completeness and relevance at scale, but the MT-Bench study identifies position, verbosity, and self-enhancement biases. Blind candidate identities, randomize answer order, repeat with swapped positions, and use dimension-specific rubrics with concrete anchors. Treat generated explanations as review aids rather than proof. Candidate output is untrusted input to the judge and may contain instructions attempting to manipulate its verdict.

diagram.title: Three evaluators, three claims
diagram.caption: Combine these signals when the task needs all three; no single score certifies correctness.

nodes.label: Executable / exact
nodes.detail: Checks a precisely specified property; vulnerable to missing tests or bad normalization.

nodes.label: Semantic similarity
nodes.detail: Recognizes related meaning; can overlook critical factual differences.

nodes.label: Rubric judge
nodes.detail: Scales nuanced assessment; requires bias checks and human calibration.

sections.title: Evaluate the evaluator
paragraphs: Create a human-adjudicated calibration set containing ordinary successes, subtle failures, and difficult boundary cases. Measure the judge's false-pass rate and false-fail rate by task slice, not merely overall agreement. If nearly every answer is acceptable, a judge that always passes looks accurate while missing every dangerous failure. Include inter-annotator disagreement so the team understands where the rubric is ambiguous rather than attributing every discrepancy to the model.

Calibration has two meanings worth separating. Rubric calibration aligns decisions with expert standards. Probability calibration asks whether items assigned a probability near 0.8 actually satisfy the criterion about 80% of the time. A judge's self-reported confidence is not automatically such a probability. Fit or validate thresholds on calibration data, then assess them on separate data. Version the judge and rerun calibration after changing its prompt or model, because evaluator drift can create an apparent product improvement.

diagram.title: Judge acceptance workflow
diagram.caption: Calibration examples and final evaluator validation must remain separate.

nodes.label: Adjudicate
nodes.detail: Experts label clear cases and resolve boundary cases against the rubric.

nodes.label: Measure
nodes.detail: Estimate false passes and false failures within relevant slices.

nodes.label: Adjust

nodes.label: Validate

sections.title: A worked comparison with statistical uncertainty
paragraphs: Run both candidates on the same examples. Pairing removes variation caused by one candidate receiving easier tasks. Consider an illustrative 200-task evaluation: both pass 130 tasks, both fail 30, candidate B alone passes 28, and candidate A alone passes 12. A succeeds on 142 tasks, or 71%; B succeeds on 158, or 79%. The observed gain is eight percentage points, not an eight-percent relative increase. Only the 40 discordant pairs determine the binary paired improvement.

Let dᵢ equal B's binary score minus A's score, so dᵢ is −1, 0, or 1. The mean difference is 0.08 and the sum of squared differences is 40. The sample variance is approximately 0.1946, giving a standard error of 0.0312. A normal approximate 95% confidence interval is 0.08 ± 1.96 × 0.0312, or about 1.9 to 14.1 percentage points. This interval describes uncertainty from sampling independent tasks under the stated design; it excludes label bias and population mismatch.

A paired binary test such as McNemar's exact test conditions on the discordant count: under equal success probabilities, B's 28 wins among 40 disagreements follow a binomial null with probability 0.5. For richer metrics, paired bootstrap resampling draws task indices and keeps both candidates' results together, as discussed in Koehn's evaluation work. Resample customers or documents as clusters when tasks within them correlate. Repeated stochastic generations add another variability level. Predeclare the primary metric, practical improvement margin, and analysis schedule; searching many slices or repeatedly checking significance inflates false discoveries.
sections.formula: Δ = mean(dᵢ); s² = Σ(dᵢ − Δ)² / (n − 1); SE(Δ) = √(s² / n); approximate 95% CI = Δ ± 1.96 SE

diagram.title: Where the eight-point gain comes from
diagram.caption: Illustrative paired counts across 200 tasks, measured in tasks. B gains 28 successes and loses 12 relative to A: net 16/200 = 8 percentage points.

sections.title: Observe both task quality and serving behavior
paragraphs: A service-level indicator is a measured quantity; an SLO is its target over a stated window and population. Define availability, time to first token, end-to-end completion latency, and task success separately. Example targets might require 99% successful transport completion over 28 days and p95 completion latency below eight seconds for a bounded workload. These are design examples, not universal thresholds. Include cancellations and timeouts in explicitly defined denominators so the dashboard cannot improve by silently dropping slow requests.

Represent a workflow as a parent trace with retrieval, model, tool, retry, and validation spans. Capture durations, errors, route, bounded version attributes, and token usage. OpenTelemetry's GenAI guidance describes these operations and token fields; pin the convention version because naming evolves. Parallel spans overlap, so summing their durations overstates wall-clock latency. Sample traces deliberately and retain aggregate metrics for all requests; a trace sample biased toward errors cannot estimate the overall error rate without accounting for selection.

diagram.title: A traced support workflow
diagram.caption: These logical stages are children of one request trace; retries and parallel branches require their own spans.

nodes.label: Retrieve

nodes.label: Validate / respond

sections.title: Make resource accounting reconcile
paragraphs: Attribute cost to all model calls in a workflow, including retries, routing, judge calls, and abandoned responses. Track provider-reported input and output usage, cached-input categories, and reasoning-token categories where available. Distinguish subsets from additive categories: cached input may already be included in total input, and reasoning tokens may already be included in output. Record the provider's accounting definitions so dashboards do not double count. Local tokenizer estimates are useful for forecasting but may differ from billing records.

With mutually exclusive billed token categories, estimated cost is the sum of category token counts multiplied by their applicable unit rates, plus other charges. Store the pricing snapshot and currency rather than embedding one permanent price. Report cost per successful task alongside cost per request: a cheaper model that triggers retries or escalations can raise task cost. Preserve usage when a call fails after generation, and reconcile periodic aggregates against invoices or provider usage reports.
sections.formula: Estimated workflow cost = Σcalls Σcategories tokens(call, category) × rate(category); cost per successful task = total workflow cost / successful tasks

sections.title: Turn evidence into canary release gates
paragraphs: Freeze the candidate before release evaluation. Require executable constraints, a predefined quality comparison, important slice checks, and load testing before exposing users. A noninferiority gate asks whether the lower confidence bound exceeds a tolerated loss, such as −2 percentage points; merely failing to detect a significant regression does not establish noninferiority. Rare severe failures need dedicated stress testing and operational safeguards because a small average-quality sample offers weak reassurance.

Following the canary principle in Google's SRE workbook, expose a limited population and compare it with a concurrent control. Randomize at a stable user or tenant boundary to avoid crossing treatments within a workflow. Gate on both absolute SLOs and relative regressions, since control and candidate can deteriorate together. Set minimum exposure, observation duration, rollback conditions, and ownership in advance. Delayed task outcomes require waiting for labels; a quiet ten-minute latency chart cannot certify next-day resolution quality.

diagram.title: A release has explicit stop points
diagram.caption: Illustrative release policy: advancement requires sufficient evidence; uncertainty can hold a stage without proving failure.

nodes.label: Offline gate
nodes.detail: Locked tasks, uncertainty bounds, constraint tests, and critical slices.

nodes.label: Small canary
nodes.detail: Stable assignment, concurrent control, immediate reliability checks.

nodes.label: Outcome gate
nodes.detail: Wait for task labels and check absolute plus relative limits.

nodes.label: Expand or roll back
nodes.detail: Increase exposure only with evidence; restore the previous complete configuration on failure.

sections.title: Close the loop without collecting everything
paragraphs: Monitor changing input mix, retrieval coverage, answer behavior, and labeled task quality. Distribution drift is a diagnostic signal, not proof of quality loss: a new topic can be harmless, while a subtle policy change can break answers without a large embedding shift. Compare recent slices against historical baselines and a stable evaluation set. Investigate whether the cause is traffic, corpus changes, a tool dependency, or evaluator drift before deciding to retrain.

User feedback is selected evidence: frustrated users and enthusiastic users may respond at different rates, and a thumbs-up does not establish factual correctness. Combine consented feedback with representative audits and delayed outcomes. In line with NIST's lifecycle risk guidance, design data governance into this loop: minimize content capture, redact sensitive fields before export, restrict access, set retention periods, and propagate deletion to derived evaluation datasets. Hashing an identifier alone does not anonymize rich conversation text. Promote reviewed failures into versioned regression tests while maintaining a fresh independent holdout.

interview.question: A new support model improves offline success from 71% to 79%, but costs 20% less per call and produces longer answers. Would you ship it?
interview.answer: I would first establish that the comparison uses paired, representative, contamination-controlled tasks and a frozen evaluator. In the worked 200-task example, the approximate paired interval is 1.9 to 14.1 percentage points, but that does not rule out critical slice regressions or judge verbosity bias. I would inspect false passes, validate with blinded expert labels, and compute cost per successful workflow including retries and longer output. After executable constraints and load tests pass, I would canary with stable assignment, concurrent control, absolute latency and availability SLOs, and predefined task-quality margins. Advancement waits for sufficient delayed outcome labels; rollback restores the full prior configuration.
followUps: How would correlated questions from the same customer change the interval?
What if the judge changes version during the experiment?
How would you detect a rare authorization violation without millions of ordinary examples?
What would make a cheaper per-call model more expensive per resolved task?

pitfalls: Treating a statistically nonsignificant regression as proof of noninferiority.
Randomly splitting paraphrases or conversations across development and test.
Optimizing against a public benchmark while describing its score as clean generalization evidence.
Using judge agreement without checking false passes on consequential failures.
Summing overlapping spans to estimate end-to-end latency.
Counting cached or reasoning tokens twice when they are subsets of totals.
Storing complete prompts by default and treating hashed identifiers as anonymization.
checklist: Specify the task population, evaluation unit, rubric, and unacceptable failures.
Version and group-split datasets; protect release and temporal holdouts.
Freeze candidate and evaluator configurations before paired evaluation.
Report effect sizes, uncertainty, important slices, and labeling limitations.
Validate judge thresholds against separate expert-adjudicated data.
Define SLO denominators, windows, and bounded telemetry attributes.
Reconcile workflow token usage and cost with provider accounting.
Predeclare canary exposure, quality margins, rollback triggers, and owners.
Audit production outcomes and apply retention and deletion rules to feedback.

flashcards.front: Why can a conversation be the correct evaluation unit?
flashcards.back: Earlier outputs and actions affect later outcomes. Scoring messages independently can hide a workflow failure and exaggerate the independent sample size.

flashcards.front: Why split evaluation data by document or customer?
flashcards.back: Related examples share information and difficulty. Keeping groups intact reduces leakage and makes uncertainty assumptions more credible.

flashcards.front: When does a locked test become development data?
flashcards.back: When developers repeatedly inspect its failures and adapt the system to them. A fresh independent holdout is needed to assess the resulting selection process.

flashcards.front: When are exact checks preferable to semantic similarity?
flashcards.back: When correctness has a precise executable definition, such as a schema or numerical tolerance. Similar wording cannot establish those properties.

flashcards.front: Why can high semantic similarity coexist with a wrong answer?
flashcards.back: A changed number, negation, or unsupported citation may leave most contextual meaning unchanged. Check consequential facts against evidence explicitly.

flashcards.front: How do you reduce pairwise judge position bias?
flashcards.back: Blind candidate identity, randomize order, and repeat with positions swapped. Residual disagreement signals uncertainty rather than permission to cherry-pick a verdict.

flashcards.front: Why is overall judge agreement insufficient?
flashcards.back: Class imbalance can make an always-pass judge appear accurate. Measure false passes and false failures on expert-adjudicated slices and boundary cases.

flashcards.front: Why compare models on the same tasks?
flashcards.back: Pairing controls task difficulty and estimates the distribution of within-task differences. Unpaired analysis throws away that structure.

flashcards.front: What is the gain when B alone passes 28 of 200 tasks and A alone passes 12?
flashcards.back: The net gain is (28 − 12)/200 = 0.08, or eight percentage points. Concordant pairs contribute zero to the difference.

flashcards.front: What does a sampling confidence interval fail to capture?
flashcards.back: It does not automatically include label errors, evaluator bias, contamination, or population mismatch. These require separate design checks and audits.

flashcards.front: Why is no significant regression not proof of noninferiority?
flashcards.back: A weak experiment may miss a substantial loss. Noninferiority requires the confidence bound to exclude losses beyond a predefined acceptable margin.

flashcards.front: Why not sum every span duration for request latency?
flashcards.back: Parallel spans overlap in time. Use the parent request duration for wall time and child spans to diagnose the critical path.

flashcards.front: How can token accounting overstate usage?
flashcards.back: Cached input and reasoning output may already be included in broader totals. Apply provider definitions and price mutually exclusive billing categories.

flashcards.front: Why combine user feedback with representative audits?
flashcards.back: Feedback is selectively submitted and satisfaction does not prove correctness. Audits estimate broader quality while minimized, governed data collection limits unnecessary exposure.
